lessons.title: Explicit binary encodings
lessons.summary: If the two encoded bytes are swapped to {2, 1}, what value is decoded?

lessons.title: Cleanup paths and status results

lessons.title: Create and join C threads
lessons.summary: If compute writes 11 instead, what is printed after a successful join?
explanation: C11 introduced threads.h; a C17 implementation may declare it unavailable using __STDC_NO_THREADS__. These fixtures require the facility and were designed for the installed GCC/runtime combination, not every C implementation. On this toolchain use -pthread when compiling and linking.

thrd_create starts a function with signature int worker(void *). The argument points to main’s still-live int; converting void * back to int * recovers its type. thrd_join waits for termination and provides synchronization before main reads the result. It also writes the worker’s return status. If join fails, abort from stdlib.h terminates the program abnormally rather than continuing with a worker whose lifetime is uncertain.

lessons.title: Mutex-protected shared state
lessons.summary: If both loop bounds change from 1000 to 250, what is the final count?
explanation: The file-scope static int count has static storage duration and is initialized to zero even without a written initializer. count++ reads and writes shared state; a mutex must protect the entire operation. Both main and the worker call increment using the same mtx_t. mtx_plain requests an ordinary nonrecursive mutex. A failed lock must not be ignored before touching shared state.

Initialize the mutex before starting work. Join the worker before reading the final count and destroying the mutex. The cast (void)unused explicitly discards the required callback argument. Checked failures abort rather than continuing unprotected; failed thread creation destroys the initialized mutex.

lessons.title: Atomic counters and memory order
lessons.summary: If the counter starts at 10, what prints after joining?
explanation: atomic_int and atomic_fetch_add come from optional C atomics. atomic_init initializes the counter before any concurrent use. Each fetch-add is one atomic read-modify-write and returns the previous value, which this example intentionally ignores.

The non-explicit atomic operations here use memory_order_seq_cst. This gives the default strong ordering; it is not a promise that operations are lock-free or fast. Atomics do not automatically turn a sequence of separate operations into a transaction. Do not replace them with volatile or introduce relaxed ordering without a separate proof.

lessons.title: Volatile is not synchronization
lessons.summary: In this single-threaded example, what changes if volatile is removed?
explanation: volatile affects how accesses to a qualified object are treated by the implementation. It does not make count++ atomic, establish inter-thread happens-before, or replace a mutex. Unsynchronized conflicting accesses by threads can cause undefined behavior even when the object is volatile.

This example is deliberately single-threaded. Replacing volatile int by int keeps its observable printed value here. It is not a demonstration that volatile and ordinary objects are identical for device or signal use; those domains need their own platform and language rules. No racy multithreaded variant is run.

lessons.title: A bounded study-session store
lessons.summary: If the first request is 0 minutes, what are the three results and final count?
explanation: This in-memory Store has two slots and used counts initialized entries. The constructor-like initializer {{0}, 0} zeroes the array and count. C does not enforce a private constructor; callers must start with a valid store and use the checked operation rather than corrupting fields directly.

add_session accepts minutes 1 through 60 only while used is below capacity. On rejection it changes neither the array nor the count. It checks capacity before indexing, preventing out-of-bounds writes. The example assumes a valid non-null store pointer and is not a file database, concurrent service or complete application.
